proposals.name: Question remains interesting if the method had failed
proposals.instruction: Judge whether the scientific question the abstract poses would still be worth an expert's attention if the proposed approach had not worked. A 10: the abstract opens a question whose answer is informative either way (does a robust classifier exist for a task; what is the functional form of generalization error vs scale; can test error be estimated without labels), so the paper is an answer to a question rather than an announcement of a win. A 5: the question is real but tightly bound to the method's success (a known task where only a better number would be reportable). A 0: the abstract's only reason to exist is that the proposed system beat a baseline; remove the win and nothing remains to report. Score the framing, not the results.
proposals.rationale: R42 and R48 and R37 pose questions (error-vs-scale form, label-free test-error estimation, existence of intrinsic robustness) that would be worth reporting under any outcome, and all sit high for the dense model and low for the scorecard. R22 and R27 are both knowledge-distillation entries whose abstracts exist entirely to report an improved number and are card-high, dense-low. A scorecard built from criteria about clarity, evidence and contribution cannot see this axis, because a pure-delta paper satisfies every one of those criteria.

proposals.name: Contribution is a reusable abstraction subsuming existing methods
proposals.instruction: Score how far the contributed object is an abstraction that other researchers can instantiate, as opposed to one artifact for one task. A 10: the abstract explicitly places existing approaches inside the new framework or applies the construction to arbitrary backbones, symmetry types, or model families, and names more than one distinct instantiation. A 5: a method with a plausible but unclaimed reach beyond its own experiment. A 0: a single architecture or representation for a single task, whose transfer is neither claimed nor structurally visible. Do not reward the word framework by itself; require evidence that other work is subsumed or adapted.
proposals.rationale: R34 says it encompasses various existing approaches and lets them be used alongside each other, R58 adapts known backbone architectures to new symmetry types and derives three model classes, and R50 generalizes boosting plus ensembling with graph propagation; all three are dense-high, card-low. R14 and R47 contribute one representation and one architecture for one generation task and are card-high, dense-low. Scorecards typically credit novelty and technical soundness, both of which a single-task artifact earns fully, so subsumption is invisible to them.

proposals.name: Introduces a portable quantity others can measure
proposals.instruction: Score whether the abstract hands the reader a measurable quantity, estimator, or phenomenon that can be computed inside someone else's system, independent of the authors' code or checkpoints. A 10: the quantity is defined in the abstract and is obviously computable elsewhere (a ratio of interpolating to optimally-tuned test error; the disagreement rate between two training runs; a named degradation phenomenon shown across many agents and environments). A 5: a quantity is introduced but is entangled with the authors' specific pipeline. A 0: no transferable measurement; all numbers are outputs of the authors' system on the authors' benchmark.
proposals.rationale: R48 (disagreement rate as a test-error estimator), R06 (cost of overfitting defined as an explicit error ratio), R55 (capacity loss demonstrated across a broad range of agents and environments) and R37 (label uncertainty) are all dense-high, card-low, and each leaves behind a measuring stick. R56 and R41 report only their own system's outputs and are card-high, dense-low. A criterion bank that scores evidence quality counts the numbers but not their portability.

proposals.name: Names the exact obstruction, then acts on that quantity
proposals.instruction: Score whether the abstract identifies the specific thing that blocks progress, states it in a form that can be checked (a complexity order, an intractable expectation, a named assumption, an explicit gap), and then shows the proposed change operating on that same stated quantity. A 10: obstruction and remedy are the same object, e.g. a stated complexity that is then reduced, or an intractable operator that is then replaced by a tractable surrogate with the same guarantee. A 5: an obstruction is named in words but the remedy is not tied back to it. A 0: the obstacle is generic (existing methods have limitations or struggle) and the method is motivated only by being new.
proposals.rationale: R34 names an O(C^2 L^5) strictly equivariant layer and delivers O(C L^4) and O(C L^3 log L) replacements; R58 names the intractable group averaging operator and replaces it with averaging over a frame while preserving exactness; R01 names Bayes-optimal policy computation as intractable and substitutes meta-learned approximate inference; R18 frames model utilization as an optimization problem and derives near-optimal algorithms. All four are dense-high with card percentiles from 0.010 to 0.293. Against these, R46 and R60 motivate with general inadequacy language. A criterion bank scoring motivation presence gives full marks to both shapes.

proposals.name: Contradicts a named default practice, explicitly
proposals.instruction: Score whether the abstract states a result that runs against a currently standard practice or widely held default, and names the default it contradicts. A 10: the standard practice is named and the contradiction is sharp (a learned component shown to be unnecessary; a component universally believed to help shown to hurt in a regime; removing training data shown to improve a target property; most modern components shown to be nonessential). A 5: a mild tension with common practice, implied but not named. A 0: fully consonant with prevailing practice; the paper adds to a default rather than testing it. Judge only the claim structure, never whether you believe the claim.
proposals.rationale: R44 argues the final learned classifier layer can be fixed with little loss, R08 shows batch normalization may prevent robustness and that deleting clean images boosts it, R29 concludes only very few modern diffusion components matter for representation learning, and R48 overturns the belief that separate training sets are required. All are dense-high with card percentiles 0.052, 0.191, 0.103, 0.284. A bank scoring novelty rewards any new method equally, so it cannot distinguish adding a part from removing a sacred one.

proposals.name: Diagnosis, intervention, and confirmation form one loop
proposals.instruction: Score whether the abstract (a) proposes a mechanistic explanation for an observed failure, (b) derives an intervention from that explanation specifically, and (c) reports that the intervention worked, so the success is itself evidence for the explanation. A 10: all three links are present and the intervention is one only that explanation would suggest. A 5: a mechanism is proposed and something is fixed, but the fix does not test the mechanism. A 0: diagnosis with no intervention, or an intervention with no mechanistic account of why it should work.
proposals.rationale: R08 hypothesizes that clean and adversarial images come from two domains, therefore applies separate normalization statistics, and the resulting robustness gain confirms the hypothesis; R28 uses synthetic tasks to localize recall and comparison as the missing capabilities and then designs a layer explicitly for those two; R16 probes for feature directions, builds control vectors from them, and checks that predictions stay feasible. All three are dense-high, card-low. R30 and R53 present careful diagnostic findings with no closing intervention and both sit card-high, dense-low. A scorecard rewarding both analysis and results scores the open loop and the closed loop the same.

proposals.name: Parsimony of the mechanism relative to problem difficulty
proposals.instruction: Score the ratio between how hard the stated problem is and how few moving parts the proposed remedy has. A 10: a hard, well-known problem addressed by a strikingly small change, and the abstract says so plainly (a single learned prior, a fixed matrix, one regularizer, averaging over a small subset). A 5: a moderate number of components, proportionate to the problem. A 0: several bolted-together modules each introduced to patch a different symptom, where the complexity of the method exceeds the sharpness of the problem statement. Penalize complexity only when it is not shown to be necessary.
proposals.rationale: R04 (a simple solution: one learned behavior prior), R44 (fix the last layer, initialize with a Hadamard matrix), R29 (deconstruct until what remains resembles a classical autoencoder), R58 (average over a small subset of group elements) are all dense-high with card percentiles 0.043, 0.052, 0.103, 0.251. R60 stacks prototype learning, a binding mechanism, and a bidirectional binding block; R22 introduces two distillation losses for two separately diagnosed symptoms. Criterion banks reward technical depth and number of components, so an elegant minimal fix is systematically underscored.

proposals.name: Enumerated contributions are conceptually distinct, not pipeline stages
proposals.instruction: When the abstract enumerates contributions (first, second, third; or firstly, then, finally), judge whether the items are independently valuable claims or merely the sequential stages of building one system. A 10: the enumerated items could each stand alone and address different questions (an expressivity analysis and, separately, a hardware efficiency result). A 5: partly independent items with shared dependence on one artifact. A 0: the list is a build log (we collect data, we label it, we train on it, we evaluate), presented in contribution grammar. If the abstract does not enumerate, score the same underlying property from its structure.
proposals.rationale: R12 lists three major technical contributions that are one pipeline (build the benchmark, use it to find neurons, turn the neurons), R17 walks firstly-then-finally through collect, label, train, evaluate, and R33 and R60 do the same; all four are card-high, dense-low or middling. By contrast R28 separates an expressivity question from a hardware-utilization question, and R08 separates normalization from capacity; both are dense-high, card-low. Enumeration is exactly the surface an explicit-criterion bank uses to score clarity and contribution count, so it over-credits build logs.

proposals.name: Claims proportional to evidence; no promotional filler
proposals.instruction: Score restraint. A 10: every claim in the abstract is one the described evidence could support, with no forward-looking boilerplate, no self-assessment of importance, and hedges where hedges are due. A 0: heavy use of promotional and futures language (paves the way, highlights the potential, extensive experiments validate the efficacy, significantly, comprehensive) carrying claim weight that the described experiments cannot bear. Mid scores for mixed registers. Judge tone against described evidence only; strong claims backed by correspondingly strong described evidence are not penalized.
proposals.rationale: R46 (paves the way for more efficient and scalable integration), R17 (paving the way for future advancements in human-agent collaboration) and R12 (extensive experiments validates the efficacy) are all card-high, dense-low. R21 claims only that the architecture is a useful inductive bias yet is the highest dense item in the slice at 0.999 with card 0.010; R25 and R06 hedge explicitly and are dense-high. Confident significance language is what a criterion for impact or significance is most likely to reward, which is precisely the over-credit direction.

proposals.name: Scope conditions and assumptions volunteered unprompted
proposals.instruction: Score whether the abstract itself tells the reader where the result does and does not hold. A 10: assumptions, ansatz, rigor level, cost, or applicability limits are stated in the abstract without being forced (naming a non-rigorous estimate as such, stating the regime of validity, quantifying the added computational cost, saying which assumptions the guarantee needs). A 5: one such caveat appears. A 0: no boundary of any kind; the method is presented as applying wherever the reader might want it.
proposals.rationale: R06 flags a Gaussian universality ansatz and non-rigorous risk estimates and still ranks dense 0.989 against card 0.023; R25 states the additional computational cost is relatively little and labels its application an exemplary use case; R50 says convergence is provable under relatively mild assumptions. All are dense-high, card-low. R39 and R11 assert scalability and success without any stated regime and are card-high, dense-low. Volunteered limitation reads as weakness to a bank that scores strength of claims and completeness of results.

proposals.name: Engages a specific prior result at the level of its assumptions
proposals.instruction: Score the precision of positioning against prior work. A 10: a specific prior result is named and the abstract states exactly how the new result relates to it in terms of assumptions, e.g. that it is a strictly stronger version because it removes a requirement, or that it refines a previously proposed taxonomy. A 5: prior work cited by name with a general comparison. A 0: prior work referred to only as a class (existing works, previous methods, traditional approaches) with a generic deficiency attached.
proposals.rationale: R48 states it is a stronger version of a prior observation because it no longer requires separate training sets; R06 positions as a more refined characterization of a named benign-tempered-catastrophic taxonomy; R43 builds directly on a named framework and specifies what it probes within it. All dense-high, card-low. R24 and R56 refer to prior work as classes with generic weaknesses and are card-high, dense-low. A related-work criterion in a bank will register that citations are present in both cases and will not register the difference in grain.

proposals.name: Resource papers show validity engineering beyond scale counts
proposals.instruction: Apply when the contribution is a benchmark, dataset, or metric. Score whether the abstract gives a reason to believe the resource measures what it claims, beyond its size. A 10: named design decisions that defend validity, such as robustness to gaming or rephrasing, structural immunity to contamination, out-of-distribution human validation, or difficulty calibration justified rather than asserted. A 5: scale plus one validity gesture. A 0: the abstract's case is an inventory (number of items, number of categories, number of models evaluated) with no argument that the numbers are meaningful. Score 5 by default if the item is not a resource paper.
proposals.rationale: R13 argues its estimator is robust to rephrasing and elongation and that its benchmark structurally avoids data contamination through continuous influx of new papers, and it is dense-high (0.756) with card 0.070. R09 presents 18K questions, 26 subcategories, 22 open and 6 closed models and is card 0.996 against dense 0.313; R17 counts 6,790 events and R12 announces a large-scale dataset, both card-high. Item counts are the easiest thing for an explicit criterion to score, so resource inventories are exactly where the scorecard over-credits.

proposals.name: Gains attributed to the stated mechanism by discriminating measurements
proposals.instruction: Score whether the reported quantities are chosen to test the paper's own explanation, not merely to total up performance. A 10: the headline numbers are on the axis the mechanism predicts should move (a physical-plausibility rate where the claim is about physicality; a synthetic capability the new layer was designed to add; the fraction of benchmarks where the trade-off should and should not help), so the reader can tell the explanation apart from a generic gain. A 5: aggregate improvements plus one mechanism-linked measurement. A 0: only totals and deltas against baselines, from which no explanation can be distinguished.
proposals.rationale: R57 reports the proportion of energetically favorable poses rising from 30 percent to 73 percent, which is the physical claim itself rather than a docking score; R28 reports closing a synthetic recall gap and a 125M hybrid crossing over Transformers, both predicted by its diagnosis; R32 reports gains split per model-based baseline and 11 of 18 datasets, matching its when-to-trust-the-model story. All dense-high, card-low. R27 and R33 report large but explanation-neutral deltas and are card-high, dense-low. A bank scoring empirical rigor counts baselines and margins, which both shapes supply.

proposals.name: Result is non-obvious given the paper's own setup
proposals.instruction: Read the setup as described, then ask what an expert would have predicted before reading the findings. A 10: the finding is one that a competent reader would not have been able to guess from the construction, and the abstract makes that gap visible. A 5: partly anticipatable. A 0: the finding is what the construction mechanically implies (a richer function class fits better; more capacity yields a better bound; a specialized design beats a generic one on its own specialty), so the abstract conveys execution rather than discovery. Do not confuse non-obviousness with unfamiliarity of the terminology.
proposals.rationale: R21 offers only that higher-dimensional attention is a useful inductive bias for logical reasoning, which is unguessable from the construction, and it is the top dense item at 0.999 with card 0.010; R48 and R42 likewise report findings that do not follow from their setups. R54, R51 and R41 all deliver exactly what their constructions imply (an independent-set design controls exposure; an influence function for a linear graph model approximates removals; more subspaces fit better than one) and all three are card-high with dense at 0.035, 0.238 and 0.083. Soundness and rigor criteria score the routine derivation as highly as the surprising one.

proposals.name: Information economy: every sentence load-bearing
proposals.instruction: Score the density of load-bearing content per sentence. A 10: no sentence restates another, no sentence describes a step the reader could infer, background is compressed to what the claim needs, and the abstract's length is set by its content. A 5: some redundancy or a short method tour. A 0: substantial length devoted to walking through architecture steps, restating motivation, or listing what was done rather than what was found. Length alone is not the target: a long abstract with no slack scores high and a short vacuous one scores low.
proposals.rationale: R21 (three sentences, dense 0.999 card 0.010), R18 (dense 0.712 card 0.043), R44 (dense 0.928 card 0.052) and R29 (dense 0.889 card 0.103) are all compressed to their claim and all sit far above their card ranks. R27 spends most of its length narrating the projection and contraction of a two-layer module step by step, R33 narrates its pipeline, and R52 enumerates five preference aspects twice; all three are card-high, dense-low. Explicit criteria reward completeness of description, so a step-by-step method tour scores well while compression looks like missing information.

proposals.name: Sheer abstract length and clause-level verbosity
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for HOW LONG AND HOW VERBOSE the abstract is, counting text only. Estimate the word count and the number of sentences, and note whether sentences are long and multi-clause or short and clipped. Anchors: 0 = under ~80 words, roughly 2-4 short sentences; 3 = ~120-160 words; 5 = ~180-220 words; 8 = ~280-330 words; 10 = over ~350 words with many long multi-clause sentences. Count only extent of text. You must NOT judge whether the length is appropriate, whether the writing is good or bloated, whether the extra text is informative, or anything about the work described. A terse abstract and a sprawling abstract of identical merit must receive 0 and 10 respectively.
proposals.rationale: Raw text volume mechanically advantages any additive rubric: more sentences means more chances for each criterion in a bank to find something to credit, independent of what the work is worth. The slice is starkly split on this axis. R20 is two sentences (~55 words) and R05 is ~90 words; R13, R36, R49, R53 and R31 are all similarly compact. Against them sit R18, R52, R30, R32, R26 and R56, each a 250-400 word block. Nothing about being able to state a contribution in three lines (R20, R49) is evidence of lower research quality, so length must be declared a nuisance rather than allowed into the bank as a proxy for thoroughness.

proposals.name: Density of quantified benchmark deltas and gain figures
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for HOW MANY explicit quantitative performance figures the abstract contains: percentages, accuracy or AP or PPL numbers, speedup multipliers such as '2x' or '10.4x', absolute point gains, dataset sizes, parameter counts, error magnitudes. Count occurrences. Anchors: 0 = no numerals reporting any measured quantity; 2 = one figure; 5 = three or four figures; 8 = six to nine figures, often stacked in a list; 10 = ten or more, including chained comparisons against several named prior systems. Score the COUNT AND PROMINENCE of such figures only. You must NOT judge whether the numbers are large, impressive, well-chosen, fairly measured, or whether their absence is a weakness.
proposals.rationale: A group that can run many models on many benchmarks emits abstracts dense with figures; a group that cannot states its claim qualitatively. R18 lists '72.14%|74.26%|68.03%' plus '2.01%|4.63%|3.03%', R29 lists '10.4x, 6.8x and 10.8x', R52 lists 92.7% / 28.5% / 49.5%, and R09 lists five separate compression-versus-accuracy pairs. At the other extreme R20, R49, R44, R31 and R27 report no measured quantity at all. Numeral density is a fingerprint of resources and of the sweeping conventions of a subfield, not of insight: R49's deconstruction argument and R20's architectural claim are number-free by design. Tagged mixed because a well-resourced group may genuinely do more thorough evaluation, so this channel must appear in the sensitivity band rather than be discounted unconditionally.
proposals.upstream_parent: compute budget and engineering headcount available for wide benchmark sweeps

proposals.name: Artifact-release advertising: code URLs, project pages, videos
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for HOW MUCH the abstract advertises released artifacts. Look for: a literal repository or project-page or video URL; the phrases 'code is available', 'codes have been released', 'we will release our code', 'data and code will be available'; named hosting (GitHub, project page, a lab or organisation domain); mention of pre-trained checkpoints or a public benchmark download. Anchors: 0 = no mention of any artifact; 3 = a bare future-tense promise with no link; 6 = one concrete link; 8 = a link plus checkpoints or data; 10 = multiple links or a link plus explicit hosting under a recognisable organisation. Score presence and elaborateness of the ADVERTISEMENT as written. You must NOT judge whether releasing code is good practice, whether the artifact seems substantial, or whether its absence is a shortcoming.
proposals.rationale: Whether a link appears in an abstract is largely set upstream of the science: some labs mandate release and staff it, others cannot clear it, and many strong theory abstracts have nothing to release. The slice is lopsided: R07, R17, R18, R24, R39, R45, R52 and R54 all carry GitHub URLs, R10 and R11 carry project pages, and R15 and R22 carry future-tense promises, while R20, R36, R13, R05 and R31 carry nothing. R54's link is under a large corporate research domain and R56's under a large institutional data platform, which is a fingerprint of organisational hosting rather than of the claim's merit. Tagged mixed because release discipline plausibly co-occurs with genuine rigour, so it belongs in both readouts.
proposals.upstream_parent: institutional release capacity and lab open-source policy (engineering support, legal clearance, hosting)

proposals.name: Enumerated contribution scaffolding and numbered problem lists
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for HOW MUCH explicit enumerative scaffolding structures the abstract: 'First, ... Second, ... Third, ...'; 'we make three contributions'; parenthesised or bulleted lists such as '(1) ... (2) ...'; 'To resolve this, we propose ... First ... Second ... Third'; numbered restatements of problems then numbered fixes mirroring them. Anchors: 0 = continuous prose with no enumeration; 3 = a single 'First ... Second' pair; 6 = a three-item enumeration; 8 = an announced count ('three major technical contributions') followed by matching ordinals; 10 = two parallel enumerations, e.g. numbered problems each answered by a numbered remedy. Score the amount of enumerative FORM. You must NOT judge whether the enumerated items are substantive, novel, or well-matched to each other, and you must NOT treat plain prose as a deficiency.
proposals.rationale: This is the canonical shape an author is taught to produce so that a reviewer's checklist can be filled in, and it maps one-to-one onto criterion-bank slots regardless of what fills them. R28 announces 'three major technical contributions' then walks First/Second/Third; R02 does the same with three ordinals after 'To resolve this'; R04 numbers two diagnosed causes '(1) ... (2) ...' then supplies two matching remedies; R41 numbers '(1) Efficacy (2) Retention'; R29 and R25 use First/Second/Finally. Meanwhile R44, R49, R13 and R05 carry no scaffolding whatever. The scaffold is a rhetorical container: identical work is scaffolded or not depending on who coached the writing, so it is a nuisance.
proposals.upstream_parent: template-following and writing coaching (advisor checklists, lab abstract templates, prior-cycle rewrite advice)

proposals.name: Importance-of-problem preamble before any technical content
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for HOW MUCH of the abstract's opening is spent asserting that the problem area matters, before any specific technical claim appears. Look for openers of the form 'X is a central challenge', 'X is critical/essential/fundamental', 'X is ubiquitous', appeals to real-world applications, industry deployment, mobile devices, drug design, or societal trends. Measure both the presence of such assertions and how many sentences elapse before the first sentence describing what the authors actually did. Anchors: 0 = the first sentence already states the specific technical object or finding; 3 = one short scene-setting clause; 6 = one to two full sentences of importance framing plus an application list; 8 = three or more such sentences; 10 = a whole opening paragraph of stakes-setting with named application domains before any method appears. Score extent of the framing only. You must NOT judge whether the problem really is important, whether the framing is accurate, or whether a blunt opening is better or worse.
proposals.rationale: Motivation prose is cheap to write, is directly targeted by any 'is the problem well-motivated / is significance established' criterion, and is uncorrelated with what follows. R17 opens 'Efficient inference in high-dimensional models is a central challenge in machine learning', R06 opens 'A critical component to enabling intelligent reasoning ... is memory', R01 spends two sentences on molecules and social networks, R45 declares implicit language 'essential', R29 invokes mobile devices, and R56 opens on the societal trend of AI-generated content. By contrast R36 opens 'We study the cost of overfitting', R13 opens 'We empirically show', and R20 opens 'We introduce the 2-simplicial Transformer' with no stakes-setting at all. The presence of a preamble tracks writing habit, not the value of the contribution.

proposals.name: Superlative competitive-claim language density
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for HOW MUCH superlative or comparative self-promotional vocabulary the abstract uses when describing its own results. Count phrases such as 'state-of-the-art', 'new state-of-the-art', 'superior to', 'significantly outperforms', 'outperforms all', 'by a large margin', 'leading performance', 'strong performance', 'excellent', 'remarkable', 'extensive experiments', 'first to'. Anchors: 0 = results described without any comparative intensifier; 3 = a single plain 'outperforms' or 'competitive with'; 6 = two or three intensified claims; 8 = four or more, including at least one absolute superlative such as 'all baselines' or 'by a large margin'; 10 = superlatives saturating the closing sentences. Score the WORDING only. You must NOT judge whether the claims are justified, whether the comparisons are fair, or whether restrained wording indicates weaker work.
proposals.rationale: Intensifier density is a stylistic dial that any author can turn without changing a single experiment, yet it directly feeds criteria about demonstrated advance. R18 claims 'leading performance', R30 'significantly improve the state-of-the-art', R41 'significantly outperforms existing methods', R42 'outperforming all open-source and close-source models', R11 'outperforms the prior arts', R01 'superior to state-of-the-art baselines', and R40 adds 'by a large margin'. Against these, R05 closes on 'near-optimal performance in many cases', R44 and R49 make no comparative claim at all, and R20 simply says the architecture 'is a useful inductive bias'. Identical evidence can be narrated at either end of this scale, so the wording must be a declared nuisance.

proposals.name: Playful idiomatic English register in title and prose
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for HOW MUCH idiomatic, playful, or rhetorically confident native-English register appears, especially in the title. Look for: puns and cultural allusions; imperative or second-person titles addressing the reader; rhetorical questions posed to the reader; conversational asides; understatement or knowing irony; informal intensifiers ('Remarkably', 'surprisingly', 'an open secret', 'we hope', 'peculiar'); joke acronyms whose expansion is a wink. Anchors: 0 = strictly formal declarative noun-phrase title and uniformly impersonal prose; 3 = one mildly informal word; 6 = a rhetorical question or one clear idiom; 8 = a punning or allusive title plus informal asides in the body; 10 = sustained wordplay across title and abstract. Score register only. You must NOT judge whether the humour is charming, whether it signals confidence, whether it is unprofessional, or anything about the underlying work.
proposals.rationale: Willingness to title a paper 'Hungry Hungry Hippos' (R35) or 'Latent Space Oddity' (R44) or 'VariBAD: A Very Good Method for Bayes-Adaptive Deep RL' (R57) is a social permission, not a research property, and it clusters hard in this slice: also 'Fix your classifier: the marginal value of training the last weight layer' (R31), the reader-addressed 'Does your graph need a confidence boost?' (R48), the idiom 'Keep Doing What Worked' (R59), 'Words in Motion' (R27), 'Intriguing Properties of Adversarial Training at Scale' (R38), plus in-body register such as R14's 'the first agent to reach the end screen in "Pitfall!"', R10's 'an open secret', and R49's 'We hope our study will rekindle interest'. Both a text-only dense reader and a human reviewer can pick this up. Tagged mixed because seniority plausibly also causes genuinely better work, so it must be reported in both the discounted and undiscounted readouts rather than silently subtracted.
proposals.upstream_parent: author seniority and first-language fluency (an established, native-English-speaking group risks a joke title; a first-time or non-native author writes defensively formal)

proposals.name: Branded acronym-colon title with method-name repetition
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for HOW MUCH the abstract is organised around a coined product-style name. Components: (a) the title takes the form 'NAME: descriptive noun phrase'; (b) the name is a capitalised or camel-cased coinage, or a backronym whose expansion is spelled out; (c) the coined name is then repeated through the body as the grammatical subject of claims. Anchors: 0 = no coined name anywhere, methods referred to descriptively; 3 = a name mentioned once, no colon title; 6 = acronym-colon title with the name used two or three times; 8 = acronym-colon title, the expansion spelled out, and four or more repetitions; 10 = additionally a starred or versioned variant ('X*', 'X-v2') or a second coined sub-component name. Score the naming and repetition PATTERN only. You must NOT judge whether the name is apt, memorable, or whether descriptive naming is more honest.
proposals.rationale: Coining and repeating a name gives any bank of criteria a stable, easily-credited referent for 'the contribution', and it is purely a packaging convention. In this slice: 'InfoGraph: ...' plus the derived 'InfoGraph*' (R01), 'LoftQ: LoRA-Fine-Tuning-aware Quantization ...' (R15), 'NORM: Knowledge Distillation via N-to-One Representation Matching' with the expansion typeset letter by letter (R18), 'SimulPL: ...' (R22), 'ImpScore: ...' (R45), 'LOKI: ...' (R56), 'WiNeRT: ...' (R03). Compare R05 ('Partitioned Learned Bloom Filters'), R13, R16, R36, R49 and R58, which name nothing and refer to their methods descriptively. R05 and R13 make sharp, self-contained claims without a brand, which shows the brand is orthogonal to the claim.

proposals.name: Submission-toolchain artifacts: hyphen breaks, markup leakage, broken links
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for HOW MANY mechanical text-preparation artifacts survive in the abstract. Count: mid-word hyphen-plus-space breaks left by copying from a two-column PDF ('fine- tuning', 'discrep- ancy', 'sur- rounding', 'uncer- tainty'); raw markdown emphasis such as **bold** left in plain text; unrendered or malformed LaTeX and escapes ('\%', '\url{}', '``quotes''', letter-by-letter math styling, a stray '\texttt{}'); malformed or duplicated URLs; dangling footnote digits attached to a sentence; missing spaces between words; curly typographic quotes and dashes mixed with straight ones. Anchors: 0 = clean uniform plain text; 2 = one artifact; 5 = two or three; 8 = four or five, including at least one broken link or several hyphen breaks; 10 = pervasive, several kinds at once. Score the COUNT of mechanical artifacts. You must NOT judge whether the text looks careless or polished, and you must NOT let artifacts colour your view of the research.
proposals.rationale: These marks are left by the production process, not the science: whether an author pasted from a compiled PDF, wrote in markdown, or had someone proofread the submission form. They are visible to any text-only model and are exactly the kind of fingerprint an unseen factor leaves. R15 carries three PDF hyphen breaks ('LoRA fine- tuning', 'discrep- ancy', 'natural lan- guage'); R41 carries 'sur- rounding' plus raw '**Efficacy**'; R18 carries the letter-by-letter '$N$-to-$O$ne $R$epresentation' and the space-less 'simpleFeature Transform'; R17 carries a broken duplicated link 'GEnBP}{github.com/danmackinlay/GEnBP'; R12 ends on a dangling footnote digit, 'emerge in our model 1.'; R22 leaves markdown bold on five preference names; R52 leaves '\texttt{UV-Attack}' and '92.7\%' unrendered. Tagged mixed because access to proofreading co-varies with resources that may also improve the work itself.
proposals.upstream_parent: authoring and submission pipeline plus access to copy-editing or proofreading help

proposals.name: Current-cycle application vocabulary versus classical theory-and-RL vocabulary
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for HOW STRONGLY the abstract's subject-matter vocabulary marks it as belonging to the currently-fashionable applied cluster rather than the classical methods cluster. High end: large language models, LLM agents, multimodal models, prompting, alignment and human preference, hallucination and factuality, quantization and LoRA, diffusion and 3D Gaussians, curated benchmark suites with question counts, named frontier systems used as tooling (e.g. GPT-4-class generators). Low end: reinforcement learning agents and control, generalization and overfitting theory, kernels, equivariance and symmetry groups, Bloom filters, belief propagation, classical architectures analysed for their own sake. Anchors: 0 = purely classical vocabulary, no current-cycle term; 3 = mostly classical with one modern term; 5 = mixed; 8 = predominantly current-cycle vocabulary; 10 = saturated, with a named frontier system used inside the method or a large new benchmark announced. Score the VOCABULARY CLUSTER only. You must NOT judge whether the topic is timely, important, over-crowded, or derivative.
proposals.rationale: Topic is not quality, but topic tracks era and community, and both a text-only dense reader and any fixed criterion bank pick it up. In this slice the current-cycle cluster is dense on one side: R22 uses GPT-4/4o to synthesise preference data, R28 and R41 and R37 are LLM-internals papers, R42 announces an agent benchmark of 6,790 events, R56 announces an 18K-question multimodal benchmark, R15 is quantization-plus-LoRA. The classical cluster is dense on the other: R57, R59, R46, R50, R51 and R55 are RL and control; R36, R13, R58 and R53 are generalization theory; R08, R21 and R60 are equivariance and geometry; R05 is a data-structure result. R06 and R29 show the pairing is not perfect, both being older-vocabulary items, so this is offered as a conjectured channel to discount, not as an established effect. Tagged mixed because a fashionable area may attract both more presentational polish and genuinely more mature machinery.
proposals.upstream_parent: submission year and subfield fashion cycle (which crowd the item was written into, and how that crowd's conventions were absorbed)

proposals.name: Mechanistic explanation for an observed phenomenon
proposals.instruction: Score how much the abstract offers a causal or mechanistic explanation for WHY an observed effect occurs, not just that it occurs. A 10: the abstract states an empirical effect and proposes/tests a specific causal hypothesis or mechanism that accounts for it (e.g., a named hypothesis, a diagnosed root cause). A 0: the abstract reports only that a change was made and a metric improved, with no attempt to explain the underlying cause.
proposals.rationale: Row R06 identifies a two-domain hypothesis explaining why batch normalization hurts adversarial robustness; row R08 diagnoses a specific 'capacity loss' mechanism behind non-stationarity in RL. Both score dense_high/card_low, suggesting the dense model rewards causal accounts that a criterion bank scoring surface features would miss.

proposals.name: Formal or provable guarantee accompanying the method
proposals.instruction: Score whether the abstract claims a property that is proven or guaranteed by construction (e.g., exact invariance, a bound, provable convergence, a conservative lower bound) rather than only an empirically observed average improvement. 10 = a stated formal guarantee/proof is central to the contribution. 0 = all claims are purely empirical averages with no guarantee language.
proposals.rationale: R21 (CBOP) takes a lower bound on a Bayesian posterior value estimate to guarantee conservatism; R46 anchors its method to a loss function such that 'provable convergence can be guaranteed.' Both are dense_high/card_low, suggesting formal guarantees are part of what the dense model perceives as quality that a criteria checklist undercounts.

proposals.name: Unifies multiple prior methods under one general framework
proposals.instruction: Score whether the abstract presents a general framework that explicitly subsumes several existing, previously-separate methods as special cases, versus presenting one more standalone method alongside prior work. 10 = the abstract explicitly shows prior approaches are special cases of the new general construction. 0 = the abstract presents an isolated method with no claim of subsuming others.
proposals.rationale: R19 explicitly frames a 'generalized spherical CNN framework that encompasses various existing approaches'; R51 (Frame Averaging) builds on and generalizes the group-averaging operator to unify invariant/equivariant architectures across GNNs and point clouds. Both dense_high/card_low.

proposals.name: Foregrounds a counterintuitive empirical result
proposals.instruction: Score whether the abstract's central finding runs against a reasonable prior expectation and is explicitly framed as such. 10 = the abstract's key result contradicts the obvious hypothesis and this surprise is explicit in the framing. 0 = all reported results are in the expected direction of improvement with no framing of surprise.
proposals.rationale: R20 shows a classifier's final weight layer can be fixed 'with little or no loss of accuracy,' against the intuition that more trainable parameters help; R36 shows test error is predictable from disagreement between two SGD runs on unlabeled data, calling it a 'peculiar phenomenon.' Both dense_high/card_low.

proposals.name: Conceptually bridges two previously distinct constructs
proposals.instruction: Score whether the abstract draws an explicit new connection between two constructs/literatures not normally treated as related, and shows the connection is load-bearing for the result. 10 = the abstract names two distinct concepts and demonstrates a substantive, non-obvious link between them. 0 = the abstract stays within one construct/literature throughout.
proposals.rationale: R36 establishes 'a new conceptual connection between generalization and calibration'; R47 connects label uncertainty (a labeling-data concept) to intrinsic adversarial robustness (a geometric concept). Both dense_high/card_low, indicating the dense model may reward synthesis that a fixed rubric may not capture.

proposals.name: Systematic ablation isolating which components are necessary
proposals.instruction: Score the depth of systematic component-by-component analysis used to identify which parts of a system are actually necessary versus incidental. 10 = the abstract describes deliberately stripping/varying components one at a time (or extensive measurement across conditions) to isolate what matters. 0 = the abstract proposes a method as a whole with no decomposition of which parts matter.
proposals.rationale: R55 explicitly 'deconstructs' a Denoising Diffusion Model into a classical Denoising Autoencoder to find which components are critical; R22 performs 'extensive measurements of the network state and its updates' during early training to quantitatively probe what drives observed effects. Both dense_high/card_low.

proposals.name: Single unifying idea versus a bundle of independent patches
proposals.instruction: Score whether the abstract's contribution is one conceptually coherent mechanism, versus a checklist of several separately-motivated fixes stapled together. 10 = one clear idea drives the entire contribution, statable in a single sentence. 0 = the abstract lists three or more independently-diagnosed problems each paired with its own fix, with no unifying account of why they belong together.
proposals.rationale: R38 (2-simplicial Transformer) is built around one idea, higher-dimensional attention, stated in a few sentences (dense_pct=0.999, the highest in the slice). By contrast R16 stacks three separately-diagnosed DNC problems with three separate fixes -- memory masking, de-allocation, sharpness control (card_pct=0.996, dense_pct=0.072), illustrating the low end.

proposals.name: Concrete, vivid endpoint achievement stated in plain language
proposals.instruction: Score whether the abstract includes at least one concrete, vivid, easily-visualized achievement stated in plain language, as opposed to only abstract percentage deltas. 10 = the abstract names a specific, memorable, real-world-legible milestone (e.g., 'first to reach X', a named game/benchmark landmark). 0 = all claimed achievements are stated only as abstract numeric deltas with no plain-language milestone.
proposals.rationale: R33 states RECODE 'is the first agent to reach the end screen in Pitfall!' (dense_pct=1.000, the single most dense-favored row in the slice); R04 (Hungry Hungry Hippos) reports concrete, legible claims like generating text '2.4x faster than Transformers.' Both dense_high/card_low.

proposals.name: Evaluation credibility grounded in method, not raw benchmark scale
proposals.instruction: When the abstract's contribution is (partly) an evaluation method or benchmark, score whether its credibility rests on a principled methodological argument (e.g., a proven statistical property, a theoretically-justified estimator) rather than primarily on the raw scale of the benchmark (item count, number of subcategories/modalities). 10 = credibility argued via methodological/theoretical grounding. 0 = credibility argued primarily via item/category counts.
proposals.rationale: R10 (GEM/GRE-bench) grounds its evaluator in a mutual-information estimator with stated 'robustness properties' against strategic manipulation (dense_pct=0.756, card_pct=0.070). By contrast R31 (PERSONALITYBENCH) and R32 (LOKI) lean on item/subcategory counts as headline evidence (dense_pct=0.188/0.313, card_pct=0.987/0.985).

proposals.name: Diagnoses a problem AND delivers a validated general remedy
proposals.instruction: Score whether the abstract both (a) identifies/diagnoses a specific failure mode or limitation and (b) provides a remedy shown to generalize across multiple settings, versus documenting a limitation without a working fix. 10 = clear diagnosis plus a remedy validated across multiple settings. 0 = the abstract documents a limitation or negative result and stops there, or only gestures vaguely at future mitigation.
proposals.rationale: R08 diagnoses 'capacity loss' and validates the InFeR regularizer as a fix across many RL agents/environments (dense_pct=0.905); R06 diagnoses the batch-norm/adversarial-training conflict and validates a fix (separate BN statistics) that gives 'much stronger robustness' (dense_pct=0.920). By contrast R02 shows neural networks 'are unable to generalize' to an implicit-logic task and offers no fix (dense_pct=0.083); R35 shows GANs 'fall short of being comprehensive models' and only vaguely mitigates (dense_pct=0.079).

proposals.name: Explicit interpretive or geometric account of internal representations
proposals.instruction: Score whether the abstract offers an explicit account of what internal model representations mean or how they are structured (interpretability, geometry, probing), beyond reporting that the model performs well. 10 = the abstract centrally characterizes representation structure/meaning (e.g., identifies interpretable directions, characterizes a latent geometry). 0 = the abstract treats the model purely as an input-output black box.
proposals.rationale: R17 uses linear probing and control vectors to show 'interpretable features are embedded in hidden states' of a motion transformer (dense_pct=0.925); R40 characterizes deep generative latent spaces via a 'stochastic Riemannian metric' to explain distortion (dense_pct=0.886). Both dense_high/card_low.

proposals.name: Imports a validated construct from outside mainstream ML
proposals.instruction: Score whether the abstract explicitly imports a concept, test, or definition from a non-ML field (psychology, cognitive science, linguistics, physics) and empirically tests whether it transfers to a model, versus staying entirely within standard ML method vocabulary. 10 = a named external-field construct is explicitly adapted and tested. 0 = no reference to any external-field construct.
proposals.rationale: R02 adapts a test 'designed to diagnose the presence of negation and disjunction in animals and pre-verbal children' to probe neural networks; R60 imports the cognitive-science 'picture-word interference' paradigm to test CLIP; R56 grounds 'implicitness' in 'principles from traditional linguistics.' All three are dense_low/card_high, suggesting this is a pattern the scorecard rewards that the dense model does not weight the same way.

proposals.name: Precise, multi-condition quantitative substantiation of claims
proposals.instruction: Score how precisely and across how many distinct conditions the abstract substantiates its central claim with specific numbers (percentages, multipliers) rather than qualitative language. 10 = several precise numbers are given across multiple distinct settings/models/datasets (e.g., three separate named multipliers or per-model percentages). 0 = claims are stated only qualitatively ('improves performance', 'achieves strong results') with no specific numbers.
proposals.rationale: R44 reports three separate, precise multiplier reductions (10.4x, 6.8x, 10.8x) across three datasets; R28 reports three separate per-model top-1 accuracy figures (72.14%/74.26%/68.03%) with matched improvement deltas. Both dense_low/card_high, suggesting the scorecard may over-credit dense enumeration of specific numbers relative to the dense model.

proposals.name: Breadth of validated scope across genuinely distinct task types
proposals.instruction: Score the number of qualitatively distinct task types/domains (not just distinct datasets within one task type) on which the central claim is empirically validated. 10 = validated across three or more genuinely distinct task types (e.g., a geometric task, a classification task, and a dynamics-prediction task). 0 = validated on a single task type only, even if on multiple datasets within it.
proposals.rationale: R51 (Frame Averaging) validates across point-cloud normal estimation, graph separation, and n-body dynamics prediction -- three distinct task types (dense_pct=0.942); R08 demonstrates capacity loss 'in a broad range of RL agents and environments' spanning sparse- and dense-reward regimes (dense_pct=0.905). Both dense_high/card_low.

proposals.name: Frames the contribution against a named, long-standing open question
proposals.instruction: Score whether the abstract explicitly names a recognized, long-standing open scientific question or intractability result in the field and positions its contribution as progress on that question, versus framing itself only against the narrow limitation of one specific prior method. 10 = the abstract explicitly names a broad, long-standing open problem (e.g., 'remains elusive', 'is intractable', an unresolved characterization) and addresses it. 0 = the abstract's only stated motivation is a specific shortcoming of one named prior method/paper.
proposals.rationale: R24 states the functional form of generalization error across scales 'remains elusive' and proposes a construction to resolve it; R41 (VariBAD) notes computing a Bayes-optimal policy 'is however intractable for all but the smallest tasks' and proposes a tractable approximation; R11 tackles the general theoretical characterization behind benign/tempered/catastrophic overfitting. All three dense_high/card_low (dense_pct=0.969/0.967/0.989).

proposals.name: Abstract length / verbosity
proposals.instruction: On a scale of 0 (extremely terse, roughly 1-3 sentences total) to 10 (extremely long and exhaustive, 250+ words across multiple sentences/paragraphs), rate how much raw length/verbosity this abstract exhibits by counting approximate sentence and word volume. Do NOT judge whether the length is appropriate or whether the underlying paper is good; score only the extent of textual volume present.
proposals.rationale: R46 is a two-sentence abstract (dense_pct=0.999, card_pct=0.010) while R08 and R56 run to roughly 230-250 words packed with sequential technical claims (R08 dense_pct=0.063/card_pct=0.866; R56 dense_pct=0.122/card_pct=0.815). Raw length tracks card_pct upward and dense_pct downward across this pair, consistent with a criteria-bank structurally rewarding more surface area to score against, independent of quality.

proposals.name: Code or project-page hyperlink presence
proposals.instruction: On a scale of 0 (no URL, GitHub link, or project page is mentioned anywhere in the text) to 10 (one or more explicit links to code, data, a demo, or a project page are given, e.g. 'github.com/...' or '...github.io'), rate how much explicit hyperlinked-artifact signaling appears in the text. Do not judge whether the linked artifact would actually be useful, complete, or high quality — score only whether a link/URL is textually present.
proposals.rationale: R03 (dense_pct=0.079/card_pct=0.950) and R04 (dense_pct=0.256/card_pct=0.964) both give live project/code links, and R56 (card_pct=0.815) links to github.com/OSVAI/NORM, while R46, R05 and R01 (all dense_high_card_low, card_pct<=0.254) contain no link at all. A lab's engineering resourcing and open-source norms leave this trace independent of the work's actual quality, though better-resourced teams may also do more rigorous work.
proposals.upstream_parent: institutional engineering resources / open-source lab culture

proposals.name: Problem-gap-solution boilerplate motivational preamble
proposals.instruction: On a scale of 0 (the text opens directly with technical content/method, no throat-clearing) to 10 (the text opens with a full templated scaffold of the form 'Recently/Despite X has advanced ... however/but Y remains an open challenge/underexplored ... In this paper we address this by ...'), rate how much of this templated problem-motivation-gap-solution rhetorical scaffold is present at the start of the text. Do not judge whether the stated motivation is compelling or the gap is real — score only the extent to which this template structure is present.
proposals.rationale: R04 opens 'Despite its importance, the absence of a metric ... significantly constrains ...' and R27 opens 'Despite significant advancements in large language models (LLMs), the rapid and frequent integration ... remains a substantial challenge' (dense_pct=0.256/card_pct=0.964 and dense_pct=0.112/card_pct=0.819 respectively), while R46 (dense_pct=0.999/card_pct=0.010) has zero such preamble and states its contribution in its first clause.

proposals.name: Explicit enumerated contribution or point-listing
proposals.instruction: On a scale of 0 (no enumeration; ideas are presented as continuous prose) to 10 (contributions or sub-concepts are explicitly enumerated with markers like 'First, ... Second, ... Third,' or '(1) ... (2) ... (3)' or repeated bolded/named sub-terms), rate how much explicit enumerative/list formatting the text uses. Do not judge whether the enumerated content is substantive or valuable — score only the extent of enumerative formatting present.
proposals.rationale: R27 enumerates '(1) **Efficacy** ... (2) **Retention**' and R52 bold-lists five named preference categories ('**translation quality preference**, **monotonicity preference**, ...') (dense_pct=0.112/card_pct=0.819 and dense_pct=0.050/card_pct=0.820), while R46 and R05 (both dense_high_card_low, card_pct<=0.093) present their contributions as unbroken single paragraphs with no enumerative markers.

proposals.name: Density of precise quantitative benchmark figures
proposals.instruction: On a scale of 0 (no numeric results, percentages, or metric values are stated anywhere) to 10 (many distinct precise numeric results are cited, e.g. several decimal-precision percentages or metric values across multiple datasets/metrics), rate how many distinct quantitative figures are packed into the text. Do not judge whether the numbers represent a genuinely strong or meaningful result — score only the count/density of numeric claims present.
proposals.rationale: R08 cites '92.7% attack success rate ... 28.5% ... 49.5% ASR' and R56 cites six distinct precision figures ('72.14%|74.26%|68.03% ... 2.01%|4.63%|3.03%') (dense_pct=0.063/card_pct=0.866 and dense_pct=0.122/card_pct=0.815), while R46 and R05 (dense_high_card_low, card_pct<=0.093) state zero numeric results. Genuinely strong empirical work can also produce this fingerprint, so it is mixed.

proposals.name: Branded method acronym or typographic coinage
proposals.instruction: On a scale of 0 (the proposed approach is described only in plain descriptive prose, with no distinct capitalized/coined name) to 10 (the text coins a distinctive capitalized acronym or stylized brand-like name for the method, e.g. an ALL-CAPS backronym or a monospace/\texttt{}-styled name, and reuses it repeatedly as a proper noun), rate how much brand-like naming/typographic emphasis is given to the proposed method. Do not judge whether the coined name fits well or whether the method works — score only the extent of branded-name coinage present.
proposals.rationale: R09 coins both 'GEM (Generative Estimator for Mutual Information)' and 'GRE-bench', R25 coins 'LOKI', and R08 typesets '\texttt{UV-Attack}' in monospace (dense_pct 0.756/0.079/0.063, card_pct 0.070/0.950/0.866 respectively), while R05 and R07 (dense_high_card_low) describe their contributions without ever naming/branding them. Better-resourced or more PR-savvy teams both brand more and may do more polished work, so this is mixed.
proposals.upstream_parent: institutional PR / lab branding practice and professional writing support

proposals.name: Epistemic hedging / tentativeness density
proposals.instruction: On a scale of 0 (all claims are stated as confident, unqualified assertions, e.g. 'we show', 'we demonstrate', 'we prove') to 10 (claims are frequently qualified with tentative/hedging language such as 'may', 'might', 'could', 'suggests', 'we hope', 'not necessarily'), rate how much epistemic hedging language appears in the text. Do not judge whether the hedging is scientifically appropriate or whether the underlying claims are more or less certain — score only the density of hedging/tentative phrasing present.
proposals.rationale: R11 hedges twice ('may better reveal', 'may not necessarily be Euclidean', dense_pct=0.020/card_pct=0.839) and R39 hedges ('may be a precursor', 'even if they are not yet sufficient', dense_pct=0.083/card_pct=0.941), while R01 ('We demonstrate that capacity loss occurs', dense_pct=0.905/card_pct=0.254) and R21 ('We empirically show ... We further theoretically show', dense_pct=0.980/card_pct=0.284) use unhedged confident declaratives throughout. Genuine result-uncertainty can also legitimately produce hedged phrasing, so this is mixed.
proposals.upstream_parent: author confidence/seniority (degree to which phrasing is coached toward assertive vs. cautious register)

proposals.name: Topic-currency / hype-cycle vocabulary density
proposals.instruction: On a scale of 0 (no mentions of currently-fashionable AI terms such as 'large language model(s)/LLM', 'agent(s)', 'diffusion model', 'GPT', 'foundation model', 'multimodal') to 10 (the text is saturated with such currently-fashionable terminology throughout), rate how much of this trend/hype-cycle vocabulary appears in the text, regardless of the underlying topic. Do not judge whether the topic is important or the work is good — score only the density of this specific vocabulary class.
proposals.rationale: R17 ('Agents powered by large language models', dense_pct=0.179/card_pct=0.990) and R34 ('Large language models (LLMs) have become increasingly proficient', dense_pct=0.188/card_pct=0.987) and R52 ('GPT-4/4o', dense_pct=0.050/card_pct=0.820) are saturated with this vocabulary, while R01, R05 and R44 (all dense_high_card_low, card_pct<=0.293) use only classical RL/generalization-theory/CNN vocabulary with zero such terms. Fashionable topics can also be genuinely more urgent, so this is mixed.

proposals.name: Explicit self-limitation or caveat statement
proposals.instruction: On a scale of 0 (the text states its claims and results with no acknowledgment of any limitation, caveat, or failure case) to 10 (the text explicitly names a limitation, negative result, caveat, or recommendation for how future work should address a shortcoming), rate how much explicit self-limiting/caveat language is present. Do not judge whether the acknowledged limitation is serious or minor, or whether acknowledging it reflects well or poorly on the work — score only whether such language is textually present.
proposals.rationale: R38 closes with 'we recommend that more research on LLMs' factuality enhancement make efforts to reduce the sacrifice of context-faithfulness' and R39 states the networks 'are unable to generalize to a task that requires implicit logic' as an acknowledged negative result (dense_pct=0.060/card_pct=0.871 and dense_pct=0.083/card_pct=0.941), while R01 and R05 (dense_high_card_low) state only positive achievements with no caveat sentence. Careful, well-mentored research programs also genuinely test and report limitations, so this is mixed.
proposals.upstream_parent: professional editorial coaching / mentorship in preempting reviewer criticism

proposals.name: Future-tense promissory artifact-release phrasing
proposals.instruction: On a scale of 0 (no mention of code/data release, or code/data described as already available now) to 10 (code/data availability is described only as a future promise, e.g. 'we will release our code' or 'code will be made available', rather than a present, already-live link), rate how much the text frames artifact release in future/promissory tense specifically, as opposed to present-tense already-available. Do not judge whether the eventual release will happen or be useful — score only the extent of future-tense promissory phrasing about artifacts.
proposals.rationale: R36 ends 'We will release our code' with no link (dense_pct=0.101/card_pct=0.773) and R52 states 'Our data and code will be available at https://github.com/EurekaForNLP/SimulPL' in future tense despite giving a URL (dense_pct=0.050/card_pct=0.820), while R56 and R08 state 'Code is available at ...' / 'code available at ...' in present tense with an already-live link (card_pct=0.815 and 0.866).
proposals.upstream_parent: submission timing pressure (last-minute submission before artifacts were finalized)

proposals.name: Mechanistic explanation of failure
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract identifies a concrete causal mechanism behind a limitation and links it to a diagnostic or intervention; score 0 when it only states a challenge and reports gains without explaining why.
proposals.rationale: R05 diagnoses factuality-driven loss of context faithfulness, while R40 links normalization behavior to adversarial-robustness failure.

proposals.name: Constraint-matched problem formulation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the method is explicitly designed around the task’s distinctive operational constraints and each design choice addresses a named constraint; score 0 when a generic method is applied without such correspondence.
proposals.rationale: R10 designs mobility into manipulation to prevent navigation failures, and R24 uses uncertainty to address model error in offline RL.

proposals.name: Component isolation and necessity
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract systematically removes or varies components to establish which are necessary and derives a simpler principle; score 0 when many components are bundled with no isolation of their roles.
proposals.rationale: R02 deconstructs diffusion models to identify essential components, while R28 analyzes separate memory pathologies before proposing targeted fixes.

proposals.name: Transfer across regimes
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when validation spans substantially different tasks, domains, scales, or unseen conditions and the abstract explains the shared source of transfer; score 0 when evidence comes from one narrow benchmark setting.
proposals.rationale: R01 spans exploration games and environments, and R34 tests imitation and task reuse across diverse humanoid behaviors.

proposals.name: Compositional integration of capabilities
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when multiple meaningful capabilities are composed through clearly defined interfaces that address interaction or error propagation; score 0 when modules are merely concatenated without an interaction rationale.
proposals.rationale: R10 integrates mobile manipulation with region-goal navigation, while R55 combines state-space and attention mechanisms to cover complementary sequence abilities.

proposals.name: Theorem-to-design alignment
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when formal guarantees, bounds, or complexity results directly justify the proposed construction under clearly stated assumptions; score 0 when theory is ornamental or disconnected from the method.
proposals.rationale: R36 connects exact symmetry guarantees to frame averaging, and R53 ties convergence guarantees to its graph-boosting framework.

proposals.name: Uncertainty-aware decision rule
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when uncertainty is explicitly represented and used to select actions, combine estimates, or define a conservative rule; score 0 when uncertainty is mentioned only descriptively or rhetorically.
proposals.rationale: R24 trades model-based and model-free estimates using epistemic uncertainty, while R35 incorporates label uncertainty into intrinsic robustness measurement.

proposals.name: Domain-structure matched representation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the representation or inductive bias encodes a structure intrinsic to the domain and the abstract directly tests that structural claim; score 0 when the representation change is generic or structurally unmotivated.
proposals.rationale: R30 encodes directional and long-range physical interactions, while R52 matches hyperbolic geometry to linguistic hierarchies.

proposals.name: Efficiency-capability co-design
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when algorithmic design reduces computation, memory, or latency while preserving or expanding capability, with concrete resource accounting; score 0 when efficiency is vague or asserted without a design mechanism.
proposals.rationale: R16 removes classifier parameters while retaining classification utility, and R43 redesigns equivariant layers to reduce complexity while enabling larger models.

proposals.name: Falsifiable hypothesis testing
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract states a sharp hypothesis and uses contrasting conditions, negative cases, or interventions that distinguish competing explanations; score 0 when it only showcases favorable aggregate results.
proposals.rationale: R07 tests logical generalization and reports systematic failures, while R27 probes GAN limitations through controlled latent-space transformations.

proposals.name: Assumption-level novelty
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract names a limiting assumption of prior methods and replaces or relaxes it through a clearly different formulation; score 0 when standard components are mainly repackaged under a new name.
proposals.rationale: R17 addresses the cluster and conservative-adaptation assumptions behind domain adversarial training, while R39 replaces the Gaussian-prior setup for unpaired translation.

proposals.name: Stress-tested validity
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract probes robustness under distribution shift, unseen inputs, perturbations, or varied tasks and identifies failure boundaries; score 0 when it evaluates only familiar IID benchmark conditions.
proposals.rationale: R31 evaluates unseen poses, views, and black-box detectors, while R40 studies robustness across normalization choices and substantially increased model capacity.

proposals.name: Intervention-backed interpretability
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when internal analysis yields a controllable intervention or actionable diagnostic whose effect is evaluated; score 0 when the work only probes or visualizes representations without demonstrating use.
proposals.rationale: R21 converts latent directions into controllable prediction edits, while R58 turns influence estimates into guidance for graph attacks.

proposals.name: Construct validity of metric or benchmark
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the operational definition is tied to the intended construct, independently validated on novel data or by humans, and accompanied by explicit limitations; score 0 when scale or automatic correlation is treated as validity.
proposals.rationale: R06 validates implicitness against human judgments and out-of-distribution data, while R38 addresses reference-free evaluation and strategic manipulation.

proposals.name: Quantified tradeoff and boundary analysis
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract quantifies benefits alongside costs, failure modes, or tradeoffs and states where the method may not apply; score 0 when it presents only broad superiority claims.
proposals.rationale: R05 quantifies the tradeoff between factuality and context faithfulness, while R44 reports compression gains together with accuracy loss and the conditions enabling pruning.

proposals.name: Abstract verbosity
proposals.instruction: On a 0–10 scale, how much extended, multi-clause, detail-heavy prose is present? Judge only the extent of verbosity, not whether it is good, rigorous, or useful.
proposals.rationale: Long, densely elaborated abstracts such as R02 and R16 visibly provide more textual material for pattern-based impressions, although verbosity itself is not research quality.

proposals.name: Result-number saturation
proposals.instruction: On a 0–10 scale, how much does the abstract contain explicit numerical results, percentages, error values, speedups, parameter counts, or performance deltas? Judge amount only, not whether the numbers are favorable or credible.
proposals.rationale: R27 and R54 contain many explicit percentages and comparative figures, while R22 contains almost none; numerical density can be predictive without establishing quality.

proposals.name: Acronym branding
proposals.instruction: On a 0–10 scale, how much are custom acronyms, stylized method names, or branded benchmark labels foregrounded? Judge only naming prominence, not whether the names are effective or deserved.
proposals.rationale: R28 foregrounds RECODE and DETOCS, while R58 foregrounds PERSONALITYBENCH and related branding; such naming conventions can influence textual salience without indicating quality.

proposals.name: Evaluation breadth
proposals.instruction: On a 0–10 scale, how much does the abstract enumerate multiple datasets, tasks, environments, modalities, or application settings? Judge only breadth of enumeration, not whether the evaluation is adequate.
proposals.rationale: R16 lists synthetic languages, OpenWebText, the Pile, and SuperGLUE, while R20 spans five modalities and many subcategories. Broad evaluation fingerprints may reflect resources that also enable genuine quality, so this is mixed.

proposals.name: Artifact-release signaling
proposals.instruction: On a 0–10 scale, how much does the abstract include explicit code, project-page, checkpoint, dataset, video, or release statements or links? Judge presence and prominence only, not whether the artifact is useful or the release is good.
proposals.rationale: R08 and R18 prominently advertise project pages or supplementary video, and R13 advertises supporting code. Professionalized dissemination can affect impressions and may also accompany better reproducibility, making this mixed.

proposals.name: Formalism density
proposals.instruction: On a 0–10 scale, how much formal mathematical notation or theory language—such as bounds, operators, metrics, asymptotic complexity, or universality claims—appears? Judge amount only, not correctness or importance.
proposals.rationale: R03 uses influence-function error bounds, while R42 and R51 emphasize formal risk or complexity analysis. Mathematical presentation style can be predictive of reception without itself being quality.

proposals.name: Literature anchoring
proposals.instruction: On a 0–10 scale, how much does the abstract explicitly anchor claims to named prior papers, methods, historical lineages, or established terminology? Judge citation and lineage density only, not whether the references are appropriate.
proposals.rationale: R05 and R49 densely position their work among named prior approaches, whereas R22 provides little such anchoring. Community embeddedness may influence textual reception and can also contribute to genuine research quality, so this is mixed.

proposals.name: Scale-resource cues
proposals.instruction: On a 0–10 scale, how much does the abstract mention unusually large models or datasets, high-resolution or long-horizon settings, extensive training, or hardware and compute constraints? Judge only resource-scale language, not achievement.
proposals.rationale: R16 mentions models up to 2.7B parameters and long sequences, while R56 emphasizes ImageNet-scale training and ResNet-638. Resource scale can signal organizational capacity while also enabling substantive quality, so it is mixed.

proposals.name: Trend-currentness markers
proposals.instruction: On a 0–10 scale, how much does the abstract use currentness markers such as “recent,” “latest,” “state-of-the-art,” newly fashionable model families, or emerging application labels? Judge only visible trend language, not whether the claims are true.
proposals.rationale: R06 invokes LLMs and recent LoRA quantization, while R20 and R58 use contemporary LMM and personality-induction framing. Timing and fashion can shape attention and research direction, and may also affect substantive work, so this is mixed.

proposals.name: Human-centered framing
proposals.instruction: On a 0–10 scale, how much does the abstract foreground human judgments, user studies, preferences, annotators, naturalistic behavior, or people-facing deployment scenarios? Judge amount only, not relevance or merit.
proposals.rationale: R35 foregrounds human preferences and GPT-generated preference data, while R53 reports a user study and R58 frames personality simulation around applications. Social salience can affect impressions and may also support genuinely useful research, so this is mixed.

proposals.name: Mechanism-to-intervention coherence
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract identifies a concrete failure mechanism and directly derives an intervention that addresses it; score 0 when the proposed method is disconnected from the stated problem or is merely empirical.
proposals.rationale: Motivated by the diagnosis-driven fixes in R08 and R23, and by R49's analysis linking factuality methods to context-faithfulness degradation.

proposals.name: Structural explanation beyond correlation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the work explains why the observed behavior follows from a model, geometry, causal structure, or formal argument; score 0 when it only reports associations or benchmark differences.
proposals.rationale: R05 connects intrinsic robustness to label uncertainty, while R32 derives latent-space distortion from a Riemannian metric.

proposals.name: Assumption–reality alignment
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the method explicitly identifies a mismatch between standard assumptions and the target setting and redesigns the method around that mismatch; score 0 when assumptions and deployment conditions are left implicit.
proposals.rationale: R09 addresses model error in offline RL through epistemic uncertainty, and R27 incorporates directional, long-range, and external interactions absent from ordinary message passing.

proposals.name: Guarantee tied to construction
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a formal guarantee follows directly from the proposed architecture or algorithm and concerns the central claimed property; score 0 when guarantees are absent, generic, or unrelated to the main contribution.
proposals.rationale: R15 proves exact invariance and expressive-power properties for frame averaging, while R28 anchors graph-boosting integration to provable convergence.

proposals.name: Claim-aligned stress testing
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when experiments deliberately test the claimed capability under difficult, shifted, unseen, or adversarial conditions; score 0 when evaluation is limited to routine in-distribution benchmarks.
proposals.rationale: R06 tests control-vector generalization to unseen characteristics, and R21 evaluates long-horizon mobile manipulation where skill-chaining failures arise.

proposals.name: Compositional abstraction
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the method represents reusable components and explicitly models their interactions to support new combinations or tasks; score 0 when it treats the task as an undifferentiated prediction problem.
proposals.rationale: R01 discovers subtask hierarchies, R16 composes interests from item characteristics, and R51 reuses learned motor primitives for unseen behaviors.

proposals.name: Interpretability with operational consequence
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when an interpretable structure is not only visualized or probed but used to modify, control, diagnose, or improve the model; score 0 when interpretability is purely descriptive.
proposals.rationale: R06 turns latent directions into controllable inference-time interventions, while R41 uses influence estimates to guide graph attacks.

proposals.name: Uncertainty-aware decision design
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when uncertainty is quantitatively represented and changes estimation, action, or conservatism in the method; score 0 when uncertainty is mentioned only as motivation or is not operationalized.
proposals.rationale: R09 trades model-based and model-free estimates using epistemic uncertainty, and R58 conditions exploration on inferred task uncertainty.

proposals.name: Resource-aware capability expansion
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the work expands expressivity, fidelity, or scale while explicitly quantifying and controlling computational, memory, or data costs; score 0 when capability claims ignore resource requirements.
proposals.rationale: R11 reduces spherical CNN complexity while increasing feasible expressivity, and R59 jointly addresses sequence expressivity, hardware utilization, and long-context speed.

proposals.name: Evaluation that isolates the contribution
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the evaluation distinguishes the proposed mechanism from alternative explanations through ablations, targeted comparisons, or multiple complementary measures; score 0 when it relies mainly on aggregate improvements over loosely matched baselines.
proposals.rationale: R04 deconstructs diffusion models component by component, and R08 separately diagnoses normalization and capacity effects.

proposals.name: Problem reframing with explanatory payoff
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the paper reframes a familiar task in a way that reveals a previously hidden structure or limitation and enables a principled solution; score 0 when it applies a standard technique without changing understanding of the problem.
proposals.rationale: R18 reframes GAN limitations as steerability over distributional shifts, while R30 formulates learned Bloom-filter utilization as an optimization problem.

proposals.name: Joint satisfaction of competing constraints
