proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the method explicitly handles several interacting requirements that would normally trade off, with the design addressing them together; score 0 when it optimizes only one requirement while ignoring the others.
proposals.rationale: R03 jointly handles translation quality, monotonicity, simplicity, key points, and latency, while R40 targets arbitrary resolution together with global consistency, local detail, and efficiency.

proposals.name: Boundary and failure characterization
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract clearly identifies where the method or underlying models fail, why they fail, and what conditions limit applicability; score 0 when it presents only unqualified success claims.
proposals.rationale: R42 carefully documents failures to generalize implicit logic, and R57 characterizes multiple regimes of overfitting rather than treating interpolation uniformly.

proposals.name: Representation matched to task geometry
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the representation or metric is selected because its structure matches the task's symmetries, hierarchy, locality, or physical geometry; score 0 when representation choice is conventional or weakly justified.
proposals.rationale: R20 matches probing geometry to linguistic hierarchies using hyperbolic space, while R19 uses 3D structural motifs and molecular geometry for protein-binding generation.

proposals.name: Transferable integration with existing systems
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the contribution is modularly compatible with established architectures or workflows and its integration preserves or expands their useful properties; score 0 when it is a narrowly isolated method with no demonstrated compatibility.
proposals.rationale: R11 presents a generalized framework that combines existing spherical CNN approaches, and R34 integrates a neural surrogate with differentiable simulation and inverse rendering.

proposals.name: Abstract verbosity
proposals.instruction: Rate 0–10 how much the abstract exhibits high length, clause density, and elaboration; judge only the amount of verbosity, not whether the research is good.
proposals.rationale: Long, densely elaborated abstracts such as R07 and R32 contrast with extremely compressed ones such as R33 and R40. Verbosity can shape perceived substance without measuring research quality.

proposals.name: Memorable title framing
proposals.instruction: Rate 0–10 how much the title uses catchy, playful, rhetorical, or unusually memorable framing; judge only the title’s presentation style, not whether the research is good.
proposals.rationale: R07 uses the playful title “Hungry Hungry Hippos,” while R04 uses a rhetorical question and R50 uses an acronym-led title. Memorable framing can attract attention independently of research quality.

proposals.name: Citation-name density
proposals.instruction: Rate 0–10 how much the abstract contains named papers, authors, years, or explicit attribution to prior work; judge only the amount of attribution, not whether the research is good.
proposals.rationale: R06 names Oh et al. and dates prior work, while R20 cites several named research lines and years; R55 also foregrounds named prior methods. A connected or senior author may leave richer attribution fingerprints, and that background can also correlate with genuine quality.

proposals.name: Quantified result detail
proposals.instruction: Rate 0–10 how much the abstract presents exact numerical results, percentages, margins, error values, or speedups; judge only the quantity and specificity of numerical detail, not whether the results are good.
proposals.rationale: R17 gives multiple attack-success percentages, R39 reports several precise benchmark improvements, and R57 lists multiplication reductions and accuracy changes. Resource-rich teams may support more extensive measurement, which can also contribute to genuine quality.

proposals.name: Artifact availability signaling
proposals.instruction: Rate 0–10 how much the abstract advertises code, data, checkpoints, project pages, videos, or other public artifacts; judge only the extent of artifact signaling, not whether the research is good.
proposals.rationale: R05, R21, R28, and R54 explicitly provide code, project, checkpoint, or video links. Resources and dissemination support leave this textual fingerprint and may also enable genuinely stronger work.

proposals.name: Trend-term concentration
proposals.instruction: Rate 0–10 how much the abstract clusters currently fashionable technical terms or named paradigms such as LLM, diffusion, NeRF, Transformer, or foundation-model language; judge only terminology frequency, not whether the research is good.
proposals.rationale: R17, R42, and R53 concentrate terms such as dynamic NeRF, LLM, latent diffusion, and 3D Gaussians, whereas older-style abstracts such as R13 and R31 use less trend-saturated wording. Community fashion can affect textual reception without being research quality.

proposals.name: Typesetting irregularity
proposals.instruction: Rate 0–10 how much the abstract contains visible markup, boldface, malformed line breaks, spacing anomalies, or other formatting irregularities; judge only the amount of irregularity, not whether the research is good.
proposals.rationale: R05 contains bold inline labels, R32 contains malformed “N-to-O ne” and “simpleFeature” formatting, and R42 contains the broken word “sur- rounding.” Editing and preparation processes leave visible traces that are unrelated to underlying quality.

proposals.name: Evaluation breadth signaling
proposals.instruction: Rate 0–10 how much the abstract emphasizes many datasets, tasks, modalities, environments, models, or application settings; judge only the breadth claimed, not whether the research is good.
proposals.rationale: R07 spans synthetic languages, OpenWebText, long-range benchmarks, the Pile, and SuperGLUE, while R47 spans five modalities, 26 categories, and 28 models; R39 cites 18 benchmark datasets. Large teams and resources can produce broader evaluations while also affecting genuine research quality.

proposals.name: Promotional intensifiers
proposals.instruction: Rate 0–10 how much the abstract uses emphatic or promotional wording such as “remarkably,” “striking,” “pivotal,” “comprehensive,” “significantly,” or “state-of-the-art”; judge only the amount of intensifying language, not whether the research is good.
proposals.rationale: R17 uses “high,” “practical,” and “significantly outperforming,” R28 uses “remarkably,” and R50 repeatedly claims “new state-of-the-art.” Such rhetoric can influence impressions without establishing research quality.

proposals.name: Template-structure conformity
proposals.instruction: Rate 0–10 how much the abstract follows a conventional problem–limitation–method–evaluation–artifact sequence; judge only the presence of this rhetorical template, not whether the research is good.
proposals.rationale: R10, R19, and R32 each closely follow a gap, proposed method, experiments, and implementation-release structure. Familiar abstract templates can make text easier to process and compare without measuring the underlying contribution.
